title: Nvidia's Huang Resigns, Iran War Fears Grow, Doomsday Date Arrives
bluf: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday with no reason given, days after admitting an affair with a woman some US officials suspect of spying for China. Iran says Hormuz stays shut until its seven conditions are met, and Israeli TV reports the US told allies to get ready for renewed war. After meeting Putin, Trump's envoys say a new round of Ukraine talks with Europeans in the room is agreed, though no date is set. Mississippi counties certify Scott Colom's Senate win today, and Hyde-Smith has reportedly conceded. Today is the 'doomsday' date from a 1960 science paper, and coverage is mostly explainers.

worldConditions.overall: Signs point back toward war with Iran: Tehran set seven conditions, tankers keep burning, and Israeli TV says the US told allies to prepare. Ukraine diplomacy moved a step, with a three way round agreed but no date. Nvidia losing its founder overnight adds a tech and China shock.
worldConditions.postureBasis: Reported US warnings to allies about renewed war with Iran, continued tanker fires near Hormuz, and Iranian threats against a US cabinet member.

updates.update: Since Nov 7 the talks track has turned to public denial on both sides, while signs of renewed war grow. Iran set seven conditions and said Hormuz stays shut until they are met. Tanker hits continue, an unclaimed strike hit Sirik, and a third US carrier is on the way.

The Abu Dhabi round ended without a ceasefire. Ukrainian sources say Russia refused to discuss territory, energy or the Black Sea on day two. The US envoys then met Putin on November 12 and say a new three way round with Europeans is agreed, though no date is set. A prisoner swap of 1,000 for 1,000, possibly 1,500, was discussed, but no exchange date has been announced.

Mississippi counties certify Scott Colom's Senate win today. The Mississippi Free Press reports Hyde-Smith conceded, and the governor and the state Republican chair put out statements on Colom's win. Alaska's ranked choice count is November 18. Funding runs out December 11.

Taiwan's defense minister said on November 10 that China is running 'area denial' drills in the Western Pacific with the Liaoning carrier group. The drills come before APEC and Taiwan's November 28 local vote. China declared no drills and calls the carrier's training routine. No new court rulings or detentions in the election interference cases surfaced on November 12 or 13.

Law 186 took effect November 9 and provincial heads began falling within a day, starting with Camagüey's governor. Washington and Havana traded public blows on November 9 even as quieter contacts were reported. The street dollar eased after topping 930 pesos.

Poland is now the front line of the shadow war in court and in propaganda. It indicted a Ukrainian man for the 2025 rail bombing, while Russia's FSB claimed a Polish spy ring in Kaliningrad that Warsaw calls disinformation. A Russian bot network moved on to Spain's election, and a Munich fair pulled Chinese drone parts.

Lula spent November 11 and 12 at COP31 in Turkey and flew to Manila, with his Finance pick still open. A court fined Meta over unequal treatment of candidates, which may feed both sides' claims about the runoff.

items.headline: Hyde-Smith reportedly concedes as Mississippi counties certify today
items.summary: The Mississippi Free Press, an independent nonprofit newsroom, ran a headline saying Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded to Democrat Scott Colom. The article itself could not be opened, so the wording and timing of her concession are unconfirmed. WLOX, a Gulf Coast TV station, also posted statements on Colom's win from Governor Tate Reeves and the state Republican chair on November 12. Counties face a November 13 deadline to certify.
items.assessment: A concession closes off the court fight both sides had lawyered up for, since Mississippi has no recount law. Watch whether the state party drops its push to set aside affidavit ballots or keeps it alive for future races.

items.headline: Young and diverse voters turned out while older Trump voters stayed home
items.summary: Stateline, the States Newsroom data desk, published a turnout analysis of the midterms. Its headline finding is that younger and more diverse voters showed up while older Trump voters did not. The article body was not opened, so county level figures are not confirmed here.
items.assessment: If the gap was turnout, not persuasion, Republicans face a different fix than the one their leaders are debating. It also means the 2028 map depends on whether these new voters come back without a Trump midterm to vote against.

items.headline: Democratic states fight the Postal Service over a Trump mail ballot rule
items.summary: States Newsroom reports that Democratic state election officials are battling the US Postal Service over a mail ballot rule pushed by the Trump administration. The fight is framed around the 2028 presidential election. The article was not opened, so the rule's exact terms are not confirmed here.
items.assessment: With Congress lost, the White House can still shape 2028 through agencies like the Postal Service that do not need new laws. Expect this to become a court fight well before any 2028 ballots are mailed.

items.headline: Election denial loses steam as Trump shifts on accepting results
items.summary: States Newsroom reports that efforts to dispute the midterm results are fading. Its headline says Trump has gone back and forth on whether he accepts the outcome. The body was not opened.
items.assessment: Fading denial claims plus the Mississippi concession lower the odds of a drawn out certification fight. Alaska's November 18 ranked count is now the last obvious place for one to restart.

items.headline: Trump tells Vance to chase fraud, not Iran talks
items.summary: On Thursday Trump posted that diplomacy with Tehran was not worth it. He said Vice President JD Vance should focus on fraud in federal programs. The same day, the Wall Street Journal reported Vance was weighing a face to face meeting with Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei, with Trump's approval. Rezaei had already told Al Mayadeen, a pro Hezbollah TV channel, that talk of a Qatar meeting was a lie.
items.assessment: Both capitals are now publicly denying the channel that Qatar says exists. That usually means each side wants the other to move first, not that talks are dead. We put the chance of a Vance and Rezaei meeting before December at about 25%.

items.headline: Iran says Hormuz stays shut until its seven conditions are met
items.summary: Rezaei said the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until Washington accepts seven conditions. Iran has not published the list. Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi say it includes lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade and ending Israel's attacks on Lebanon. Araghchi said the strait could reopen within two days of a deal.
items.assessment: Tying Hormuz to Lebanon makes Israel's Lebanon policy a bargaining chip in US and Iranian talks. That gives a new Israeli government a reason to slow down there, or a reason to escalate to spoil a deal.

items.headline: US reportedly tells Israel and Gulf states to prepare for renewed war
items.summary: Israel's public broadcaster Kan reported that US Central Command told Israeli military officers in the US to get ready for renewed operations against Iran. An unnamed US official said Gulf states got the same message. Two US aircraft carriers are in the region and a third, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is due in the Arabian Sea next week.
items.assessment: A third carrier arriving while Trump calls the war over suggests the blockade is meant to be backed by a credible strike threat during the lame duck months. The report reached us through Hawar, a Kurdish outlet in Syria, so treat details as unconfirmed.

items.headline: Iranian media report an 'enemy' strike on Sirik near Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's state news agency IRNA said Sirik, a coastal town in Hormozgan province, was hit by an enemy military strike late Thursday. It did not name the attacker or give damage. Iran International, a London based opposition channel, said residents heard several explosions. No one has independently confirmed it.
items.assessment: Sirik sits on the coast Iran uses to control ship traffic east of the strait. A strike there, if confirmed, would target the routing system Iran uses to police tankers, not its nuclear program.

items.headline: Guards call two tanker fires an 'accident' on an unauthorized route
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers carrying more than four million barrels of oil caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. They blamed an accident after the ships used a route Iran had not approved. A day earlier the Guards said three tankers hit mines on such a route. The UK naval monitor UKMTO reported the tanker Dominica Prosperity was struck by a projectile on Wednesday, with the crew safe.
items.assessment: The Guards are framing every hit as the ship's own fault for ignoring Iranian routing. That builds a legal style story that Iran is managing traffic, not attacking it, which insurers and lawyers may later have to answer.
items.source: Times of Israel live blog, AP

items.headline: Clerical body calls leaving the nuclear treaty an 'unavoidable necessity'
items.summary: Iran's Assembly of Experts, the clerical council that chooses the supreme leader, said considering withdrawal from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty is now unavoidable, according to state TV. Last week the idea came from hardline lawmakers. Iran says its program is civilian, though it has enriched uranium close to weapons grade.
items.assessment: The idea has moved from backbench lawmakers to the body that picks the next leader. That raises the price of any deal, because Tehran can now offer to stay in the treaty as a concession.

items.headline: Iraq's prime minister reportedly warned of a US plan to invade via Iraq
items.summary: An unnamed Iraqi outlet, relayed by India's The Week, said Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi told a closed meeting of Shia party leaders about a leaked US war plan. One scenario reportedly had US ground forces cross from Iraq into Khuzestan, Iran's oil province next to Basra. Al-Zaidi reportedly said Iraq will stay neutral and used the leak to warn militia leaders. Neither government has commented.
items.assessment: Whether or not the plan is real, the leak helps al-Zaidi. It tells militias that attacking US targets could turn Iraq into a battlefield, which supports his push to disarm them.

items.headline: Trump warns Iran over threats to Treasury Secretary Bessent
items.summary: Trump told Salem News Channel that Iran would not last long if it killed a senior US official. He spoke after Iranian threats against Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who runs the sanctions campaign. Bessent was moved from his home near Washington to a US military base. Trump gave no timetable or specific response.
items.assessment: Bessent is the face of the economic war, so threats against him show Tehran sees sanctions, not bombs, as the main fight now. A plot against a cabinet member on US soil would be the most likely trigger for heavy new strikes.

items.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser Hospital kills at least six
items.summary: An overnight Israeli strike hit Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, one of Gaza's last working hospitals. Gaza's Health Ministry said the dead included a surgeon and a 13 year old boy. The army and the Shin Bet security service said the target was Muhammad Abu Ismail, Hamas's Khan Younis commander. His fate is unclear, and another strike hit a car outside Shifa Hospital.
items.assessment: The caretaker government is still striking at a high level while it can. A new government led by Gadi Eisenkot would inherit these rules of engagement and the legal exposure that comes with them.
items.source: Times of Israel live blog, AP

items.headline: Likud blocks Liberman from the defense committee as Katz claims war powers
items.summary: Defense Minister Israel Katz said the caretaker government needs no opposition approval for military action. Likud then blocked a vote to make Avigdor Liberman chair of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee. The vote moved to Monday, so Liberman cannot see classified material yet. Reports say Netanyahu pushed for action on Iran over his security chiefs' objections.
items.assessment: This opens a gap of several days when parliament has no working oversight of war decisions. Liberman's warning about being dragged into war suggests the opposition fears an Iran strike timed for that gap.
items.source: Times of Israel live blog, citing Haaretz

items.headline: Arab parties and Haredi UTJ reportedly discuss cooperating
items.summary: Reports late Thursday said Arab parties and United Torah Judaism, an ultra Orthodox party, discussed working together. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said his bloc will form a government after painful compromises. Miriam Peretz said her son, a lawmaker in Eisenkot's Yashar party, would quit if Raam or the Joint List joins. Netanyahu and Eisenkot also held a joint security briefing.
items.assessment: An Arab and Haredi link would let Eisenkot add both groups without either being the sole partner the right can attack. But it would cost him on the draft issue and with members of his own list.

items.headline: Eisenkot's Syria terms: partial withdrawal, but Turkey and Russia must leave
items.summary: A Syria TV analysis says Eisenkot wants a stronger version of the 1974 truce line deal with Damascus. He treats ground Israel took since December 2024 as bargaining chips, unlike Netanyahu, who treats it as permanent. His key condition is the full exit of Turkish and Russian forces from Syria.
items.assessment: Making Turkey's exit the price of a deal turns Israel and Syria talks into an Israel and Turkey problem. That could stall any agreement no matter who governs in Jerusalem.

items.headline: France bars settler leader Yossi Dagan, Israel bars Mélenchon
items.summary: France refused entry to Yossi Dagan, head of a West Bank settler regional council, at a Paris airport. The French Foreign Ministry cited his active role in settlement policy. Israel called it completely unacceptable. Israeli minister Gideon Saar then barred French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon over his support for Gaza.
items.assessment: Travel bans are becoming a two way tool between Israel and European states. Barring a leading French candidate puts Israel inside France's 2027 election debate.

items.headline: Outpost demolished as settlers attack a village near Ramallah
items.summary: Settlers attacked Atara near Ramallah, injuring a 67 year old man and damaging cars, Palestinian media and the Red Crescent said. Overnight, Israeli Border Police demolished the Kfar Tarfon outpost and seized two vehicles, settler activists said. The same activists say over 200 unauthorized outposts went up during the last government's four years.
items.assessment: Police are already acting against outposts in the caretaker period. Settler groups are counting their gains now, to defend them against an Eisenkot government.

items.headline: More than 50 states and groups demand winter supplies for Gaza
items.summary: The UK, Qatar and Jordan led more than 50 countries and organizations in urging Israel to let in shelter, fuel, water and health supplies at once. They warned of hypothermia and waterborne disease as winter starts. Israeli strikes continue despite last year's ceasefire with Hamas.
items.assessment: Qatar is co leading this while it mediates between Washington and Tehran. That shows Doha keeping Gaza linked to its wider mediation role.

items.headline: US and French military chiefs visit Damascus, first French warship arrives
items.summary: A US delegation led by Admiral Liam Hollen, head of the anti ISIS coalition task force, met Syria's defense minister Morhaf Abu Qasra. A French naval team arrived on the frigate Surcouf and met Syria's navy commander. Syrian state agency SANA called it the first French military ship visit to Syria. No agenda was released.
items.assessment: A French warship on the Syrian coast is a quiet bid for influence near Russia's old naval base at Tartus. It also gives Damascus Western cover as Israel demands Turkish and Russian forces leave.

items.headline: Kurdish students march over cuts to Kurdish lessons in northeast Syria
items.summary: Students in Qamishlo, Hasakah, Rmelan and Girkê Legê protested a decision limiting Kurdish teaching to three lessons a week. They want Kurdish made an official language in the constitution. The report comes from Hawar, the news agency of the Kurdish led administration. Residents also complain of fuel prices and low wages as winter starts.
items.assessment: Language is where the deal to fold the Kurdish led region into the Syrian state is showing strain. School protests are a lower risk way for Kurdish leaders to push back than armed resistance.

items.headline: ISIS cells target Syria's main north to south highway
items.summary: Small ISIS cells keep hitting security posts along the M5 highway between Aleppo and Damascus. On November 5 a rocket propelled grenade hit a highway security building in Maarat al-Numan. Four highway police died in an October ambush east of Hama. Officials say the aim is to stretch forces thin, not hold ground.
items.assessment: The M5 is where Syrians judge whether the new government can keep them safe. Hit and run attacks there cost ISIS little and erode trust in Damascus as foreign investors arrive.

items.headline: Iraq orders probe of fuel theft in a militia controlled zone
items.summary: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered a committee to investigate fuel siphoned from pipelines at Jurf al Sakhar, south of Baghdad. Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran backed militia, controls the area and keeps outsiders out. Satellite images from 2021 to 2026 show tanker trucks repeatedly parked at four illegally tapped pipeline sites. A separate probe covers crude smuggled to Iran and Afghanistan.
items.assessment: Going after the money is a safer route to disarming Kataib Hezbollah than going after its guns. The group has refused to disarm, and smuggling income is what lets it refuse.

items.headline: Iraqi aide: no militia disarmament deal this year
items.summary: Yousif al-Dunainawi, an adviser to the prime minister, told a Chatham House conference in London that there will be no disarmament deal with Iran backed militias this year. National Security Adviser Qasim al-Aboudi said the plan will move step by step toward the June 30, 2027 deadline. He said two groups remain rigid and one is flexible.
items.assessment: Saying this in London, to a Western audience, lowers expectations before Washington pushes again. It also signals Baghdad will not use force against holdouts while war with Iran could restart.

items.headline: UN renews Houthi sanctions as Saudi Arabia shoots down more drones
items.summary: The UN Security Council voted unanimously to extend sanctions on Yemen's Houthis to November 14, 2027 and condemned their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi led coalition said it downed drones over Riyadh and the Eastern Province. The Houthis claimed hits on an East West pipeline pumping station and on Aramco sites, without evidence.
items.assessment: Russia and China let a resolution condemning Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia pass. That suggests even Tehran's partners want the Saudi front contained.

items.headline: Egypt: Mada Masr editor's retrial delayed over bid to remove the judge
items.summary: A Cairo court postponed the retrial of Lina Attalah, editor of the independent site Mada Masr, to November 18. Her lawyers asked to remove judge Mohamed Mubarak, who also ordered the site closed and fined her in a separate case on October 27. She was sentenced in absentia to a year in prison for false news and running an unlicensed site, and says she was never notified.
items.assessment: The case shows licensing law now does the work that terrorism charges once did against Egyptian journalists. A ruling on the judge will show whether courts will police their own procedure.

items.headline: Turkey: steel group chair under house arrest after blast killed 19
items.summary: A court put the chair of HABAŞ, a large Turkish steel and industrial gas group, under house arrest. Nine people were jailed over the explosion at its İzmir steel plant, which killed 19. Bianet, an independent Turkish outlet, earlier reported the company's own report showed rising workplace accidents.
items.assessment: Turkey is hosting the COP31 climate summit while a heavy industry disaster plays out at home. Prosecuting a big industrial owner is rare and will test how far courts go against business allies of the government.

items.headline: Witkoff says a new three way round is set, with Europeans in the room
items.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in the Kremlin on November 12, a day after the Abu Dhabi round ended. Witkoff said the US, Russia and Ukraine format was restarted and a new meeting is agreed, with European representatives taking part. He gave no date or place. Finland's president Alexander Stubb spoke of a technical meeting with Europe included "in the coming weeks".
items.assessment: Ukrainian sources told RBC-Ukraine that Russia refused on day two to discuss a ceasefire, territory, energy or the Black Sea. Bringing Europe in may move the talks toward Moscow's goal of rewriting Europe's security rules, which is what Kyiv privately complains about.

items.headline: Putin wants a second 'humanitarian mission', this time in contested Kostiantynivka
items.summary: Putin proposed a joint evacuation from Kostiantynivka, a Donetsk region city, modeled on the earlier Oleshky mission. He says 400 to 500 civilians remain and foreign journalists should watch. Unlike Oleshky, Ukrainian units still hold the city's northern and western edges. Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the point is to show who really controls the city.
items.assessment: A filmed evacuation would serve as proof of Russian control over a city that is still contested, a useful card on the eve of talks about borders. Zelensky adviser Dmytro Lytvyn warns it could cover troop rotation, as a Ukrainian drone filmed in Oleshky. No earlier report had flagged hundreds of civilians trapped there.

items.headline: Drone strike on Volgograd refinery kills four as 467 drones head for Moscow
items.summary: Ukrainian drones set fire to the Lukoil refinery in Volgograd overnight, killing four workers, the regional governor said. Lines formed at city gas stations and prices rose overnight. Moscow's mayor said 467 drones flew toward the capital region, and all four Moscow airports paused flights.
items.assessment: The strike came hours after Putin met the US envoys, so Kyiv is keeping its pressure on Russian fuel while talks restart. A monitoring channel counts this as the 13th hit on the same plant, which suggests repairs cannot keep pace.

items.headline: Ukraine hits a Russian missile ship and the Ust-Luga port on the Baltic
items.summary: Ukraine's security service (the SBU) said its drones hit the small missile ship Naro-Fominsk near Gogland Island in the Gulf of Finland. A separate strike set a large fire at Ust-Luga, Russia's main Baltic export port near Estonia. Pro war bloggers claimed three helicopter crews died there, which officials have not confirmed.
items.assessment: Strikes this close to Finland and Estonia pull NATO's Baltic neighbors into the war zone and raise insurance and shipping risk for oil leaving the Baltic. Expect Moscow to cite them when it accuses the Baltic states of helping Kyiv.

items.headline: Insuring Russian data centers against drones now costs up to 100 times more
items.summary: Russian business daily Kommersant reports that insurance for data centers jumped from about 0.03% of property value to 1 to 5%. The jump followed Ukrainian drone hits on Yandex, Sberbank and VK sites in October. The central bank's own reinsurer set a 1% base rate. Companies are cutting cover or excluding war risks.
items.assessment: This is a quiet tax on Russia's AI and cloud ambitions. Uninsured data centers make lenders nervous, so drone strikes may slow Russian tech investment more than they slow the servers.

items.headline: Seized Western firms are paying billions of rubles to a Putin war fund
items.summary: Bloomberg found that Russian units of foreign companies placed under state 'temporary administration' sent money to Putin's People's Front, which buys drones and gear for troops. AkzoNobel's former unit gave about 2 billion rubles, and units of Metro, AB InBev Efes, DKC, Can-Pack and Rockwool paid too. AkzoNobel says it learned of this from the media.
items.assessment: Western shareholders' seized assets now fund the army directly. That gives European governments a fresh reason to keep frozen Russian state money as compensation, and gives firms still in Russia a reason to leave fast.

items.headline: Lawyers publish Russia's secret list of 3,000 suspected 'extremists'
items.summary: The rights group Department One obtained an unpublished register kept by Rosfinmonitoring, Russia's financial watchdog, and made it searchable. It lists more than 3,000 people, including journalist Leonid Parfenov, musician Boris Grebenshchikov and director Vitaly Mansky. People on it can have bank accounts frozen with no public notice.
items.assessment: A hidden list lets the state punish exiled critics through their banks without a court case. Its publication also hands Western banks a ready list of people who may be wrongly flagged in shared compliance databases.

items.headline: Second car bomb kills a colonel on the same St Petersburg road
items.summary: A car exploded on Kolpinskoye Highway in St Petersburg on November 12, killing an army colonel. The same road saw a bombing that killed a lieutenant colonel in August. Local outlet Fontanka says the suspect fled via Istanbul to Moldova, and Russian media claim the explosives came over the border by balloon.
items.assessment: The Moldova route gives Moscow a pretext to press Chisinau, which it already accuses of serving Western spies. Two attacks on one street suggest the officer housing there is poorly protected.

items.headline: Lawyer for political prisoners gets 12 years for treason
items.summary: A Kaliningrad court gave Maria Bontsler, a 66 year old lawyer who defended political prisoners, 12 years for treason after a closed trial. Her son says officers offered a lighter sentence if she testified against a colleague. On the same day an appeals court upheld the 11 year sentence of Pskov opposition politician Lev Shlosberg.
items.assessment: Jailing defense lawyers removes the last people who can see inside closed trials. That makes future treason cases even harder to check from outside.

items.headline: Belarus: the man who started 2020's protests now attacks his wife's office
items.summary: Siarhei Tsikhanouski, freed in June 2025 under a US deal with Lukashenko, now streams attacks on his wife Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, the exiled opposition leader. He says she lost legitimacy and misused grant money. He wants a new 'united office' with leaders elected each year.
items.assessment: Analysts expect him to win an audience but not to unseat her. The feud still helps Minsk, because a split opposition is harder for Western diplomats to deal with as Washington keeps talking to Lukashenko.

items.headline: New: Armenia loses its vote in the Russia led alliance over unpaid dues
items.summary: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Armenia lost its voting rights in the CSTO, the Russia led military alliance, because it has not paid fees since 2024. The same day Armenia's president signed the US backed transit route deal (TRIPP) into law after a 63 to 32 vote. Pashinyan also met Erdogan on opening the Turkish border.
items.assessment: Moscow is choosing a quiet paperwork exit over a dramatic expulsion. That keeps Armenia formally inside while Yerevan builds the US and Turkish links that make the alliance irrelevant to it.

items.headline: Georgia's parliament backs ending recounts in small disputes
items.summary: Georgia's parliament passed election law changes in a first reading, 79 to 10. The central election body would declare results within 15 days instead of 26, and recounts would end where fewer than five polling stations are affected. An opposition MP says the plan lets the ruling party control the vote.
items.assessment: The same week, two senior Orthodox bishops said the government had lost its ability to govern and should stop spying on clergy. Church dissent matters more in Georgia than opposition protest, because the church is the country's most trusted institution.

items.headline: New: Zelensky wants a say in Europe's envoy as Dublin summit opens
items.summary: EU leaders meet informally in Dublin today, November 13, on who should speak to Putin for Europe. Italy's Giorgia Meloni wrote to Council president Antonio Costa warning a divided Europe helps those dragging out the war, and floated Mario Draghi. A Politico source says Zelensky wants the final pick agreed with him. Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania and Sweden were angry at Finland and Norway's leaders calling Putin alone.
items.assessment: Diplomats expect no single envoy today, only an understanding, with a decision on December 17. A Kyiv veto over Europe's negotiator would make it harder for Moscow to split Europe from Ukraine, and harder for Europe to act as a neutral broker.

items.headline: Russia's FSB claims it broke a Polish spy ring in Kaliningrad
items.summary: On Poland's Independence Day, Russia's FSB security service said it caught two agents of Polish intelligence in Kaliningrad and banned seven Poles from Russia. Poland's security services called it a provocation and disinformation. Polish fact checkers OKO.press said the Polish phone texts read like translations from Russian.
items.assessment: Former Polish security spokesman Stanislaw Zaryn expects Moscow to use the claim to back earlier talk of a Polish plot against Kaliningrad. That gives Russia a ready story if it moves troops or closes the border there.

items.headline: Poland indicts a Ukrainian man over the 2025 rail bombing for Russia
items.summary: Prosecutors charged a Ukrainian man, named only as Volodymyr B., with sabotage and spying for Russian intelligence. They say he helped plant C4 explosive on the Warsaw to Lublin line in November 2025. The two alleged bombers, also Ukrainians, fled to Belarus and remain wanted.
items.assessment: Russia keeps hiring Ukrainians for attacks in Poland. That feeds Polish resentment of Ukrainian refugees, which may be as much the goal as the damage itself.

items.headline: Russian bot network targets Spain's election with fake Reuters covers
items.summary: The Russian network known as Matryoshka is spreading fake videos and magazine covers made to look like Reuters and AFP. They claim aid to Ukraine is ruining Europe and push Spain leaving the EU or Catalan independence.
items.assessment: Pushing Catalan secession revives a wound Moscow has used before. The goal looks less like a result for one party and more like lowering trust in the vote.

items.headline: New: Russian activist banned from Schengen after refusing German spies
items.summary: German intelligence officers questioned a Russian activist after passport control and offered her a cooperation deal. She refused and was then put on the Schengen entry ban list. An exiled opposition figure has started advising anti war Russians on how to handle such approaches.
items.assessment: Earlier editions noted Germany interviewing arriving Russians. A ban after refusal turns 'voluntary' talks into pressure, which hands Kremlin media a story about Europe punishing dissidents.

items.headline: Munich trade fair pulls Chinese antennas found in Russian attack drones
items.summary: After questions from The Insider, the Electronica fair in Munich removed GNSS satellite antennas made by China's Harxon. The antennas reportedly go into Russia's Geran attack drones. Harxon's parent BDStar is under US sanctions.
items.assessment: Drone parts are being sold openly at Europe's biggest electronics fair. That shows EU sanctions checks still depend on journalists, not regulators.

items.headline: Record Warsaw march turns into a rally against Tusk
items.summary: City officials counted about 250,000 people at the November 11 Independence Day march, while organizers claimed 500,000. Marchers backed President Karol Nawrocki and opposed Prime Minister Donald Tusk over the Constitutional Tribunal dispute. There were few incidents.
items.assessment: A crowd this size shows the court fight now mobilizes the right on the street, not just in parliament. That raises the cost for Tusk of any 'constitutional reset' before the 2027 vote.

alsoNoted.headline: Polish deputy foreign minister Bartoszewski charged over missing millions of zloty
alsoNoted.note: He denies the charges.

alsoNoted.headline: Germany, France and the UK demand Russia free three former OSCE staff
alsoNoted.note: The OSCE is Europe's main security forum. The three have been jailed since 2022.

alsoNoted.headline: Finland and Norway plan to bar Russian athletes while the war lasts
A sports court orders Russia back into international hockey, Canada pushes back
Last of three tankers with Russian diesel for the US turns back mid Atlantic
alsoNoted.note: New since the earlier 'stuck at sea' item: none of the promised diesel has reached the US.

items.headline: Albania's student protests turn violent over a Trump family linked resort
items.summary: Protests in Tirana began over a luxury hotel linked to the Trump family planned inside a nature reserve. After more than 150 days they have become a movement against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government. On November 7 protesters threw stones and Molotov cocktails at the prime minister's office, and police used tear gas. Students also shoved out the opposition Democratic Party, carrying a banner saying both Rama and Berisha belong in jail.
items.assessment: Jared Kushner, Trump's son in law, has been publicly tied to Albanian resort plans. He is also negotiating Ukraine's future, so this unrest could become a reputational problem for the US envoy. The students' rejection of both main parties mirrors Serbia, where a student list just won power.
items.source: L'Espresso, with Novaya Gazeta Europe reportage (Nov 12)

items.headline: Serbian machine maker sold Russia €27.5 million in tools after 2022
items.summary: An investigation led by RFE/RL found Serbian firm Grindex kept selling machine tools to Russia after the invasion. Some reached Rostec, Russia's state defense and aerospace group, through middlemen. Serbia's trade ministry says it never licensed dual use exports from Grindex.
items.assessment: This lands on Serbia's incoming student led government, which calls Russia a 'traditional partner'. How it handles the case will be an early test for Brussels of whether Belgrade will align with EU sanctions.
items.source: The Insider (citing an RFE/RL led investigation)

items.headline: Serbia's winning Student List argues over who really decides
items.summary: Serbia's new majority, the Student List, has not yet named a prime minister or speaker. Students say university assemblies, called plenums, will help pick the speaker, premier and ministers alongside the MPs. One future MP told Vreme magazine that some decisions cannot wait for a plenum. Candidate Dejan Soskic said MPs legally own their seats.
items.assessment: Deciding by student assembly is the movement's identity but also its weak point. Delays give Vucic time before the presidential vote due at year's end, and a split would be the first thing his camp exploits.

items.headline: EU plans tough brakes on new members, starting with Montenegro
items.summary: Montenegro has closed 23 of 33 negotiating chapters and hopes to sign its accession treaty in June 2027. The Commission now proposes safeguards that would let the EU suspend a new member's funds and Council votes for up to 15 years. France, Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands back them, while Greece and Spain oppose.
items.assessment: Montenegro may become the test case for 'second class' membership that would later apply to Ukraine, Moldova and Albania. That could cool pro EU feeling in the region just as Brussels needs it.

alsoNoted.headline: Semafor: US ambassador nominee to Azerbaijan allegedly promoted sanctioned Bosnian Serb leader Dodik
alsoNoted.note: Nominee Alexander Alden. Former US official Jim O'Brien questioned his judgment.

alsoNoted.headline: Novaya Gazeta reporter's two days in Tirana during the protests
Azerbaijan, Georgia, Turkey and Bulgaria sign a green power corridor to Europe
alsoNoted.note: Signed at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya.

items.headline: Beijing media: after Jensen Huang, Washington will target more tech chiefs
items.summary: Global Times, a Communist Party tabloid, ran a commentary on November 13 after Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang stepped down. It says his exit started with reports about his private life but turned into a wider US campaign against tech leaders with China ties. A November 11 piece in the same paper said the case holds too many China linked 'coincidences' to be accidental.
items.assessment: Beijing is framing the exit as political targeting, not espionage. That framing lets it warn other foreign executives before APEC that Washington, not China, is the risky partner.

items.headline: China's car exports jump 68% while sales at home fall again
items.summary: China shipped 932,000 passenger cars abroad in October, up 68% on a year earlier, according to the China Passenger Car Association, an industry body. Sales at home fell 27% to 1.65 million, the twelfth monthly drop in a row. The association's secretary general said the Middle East should drive export growth next year.
items.assessment: China is pushing its unsold cars onto foreign markets, which feeds the trade fights Xi will face at APEC. Betting on Gulf buyers during a war near Hormuz is a risky plan.

items.headline: Beijing offers to buy Papua New Guinea's gas after Taiwan walked away
items.summary: China said it is willing to buy more liquefied natural gas from Papua New Guinea and deepen trade. The offer came days after Taiwan closed its office in the Pacific country and stopped buying its gas on the spot market. Washington had already voiced concern over Taiwan's move.
items.assessment: Taipei's use of gas purchases as leverage handed Beijing an easy win. Small Pacific states now see that pressure from Taiwan can be replaced by Chinese money within days.

items.headline: Xinhua courts Indonesia's state news agency on artificial intelligence
items.summary: Antara, Indonesia's state news agency, is exploring artificial intelligence cooperation with Xinhua, China's state news agency. It builds on a long running content sharing deal between the two. The report appeared in the China Global South Project's November 9 listing.
items.assessment: Shared newsroom tools can quietly shape what wire copy reaches Indonesian readers. Watch for Xinhua material showing up unlabeled in Antara's feed.

alsoNoted.headline: Global Times marks 25 years in the World Trade Organization: 'Shanghai signs deals, Washington signs sanctions'
alsoNoted.note: Sets up Beijing's 'open China versus closed America' message for APEC in Shenzhen, November 18 to 19.

alsoNoted.headline: Global Times cheers Japan's 'Climate Villain Award' at the COP31 climate talks
alsoNoted.note: Beijing keeps hitting Tokyo on soft issues as no Xi and Takaichi meeting is planned.

items.headline: North Korea changes its flag for the first time since 1948
items.summary: North Korea's revised constitution changes the flag's shape from a ratio of 1 to 2 to about 1 to 1.65. NK News says the white bands are also thicker. Analysts link the change to Kim Jong Un's push for a separate national identity from the South.
items.assessment: This fits Kim's policy of treating South Korea as a foreign state, not a lost half of one nation. Symbols are being rewritten so unification talk loses its footing at home.

items.headline: Kim visits a new east coast naval base as a second site appears
items.summary: Kim Jong Un inspected construction of a new naval base on North Korea's east coast. NK Pro, the analysis service of the specialist site NK News, identified a second major naval project at the Thongchon missile base. Seoul's defense chief said the South still leads militarily but the North is closing the gap.
items.assessment: Two new bases point to a navy built to carry missiles, not just guard the coast. That adds pressure on South Korea and Japan to fund more sea defenses.

items.headline: North Korea puts its Mexico embassy up for sale
items.summary: Pyongyang listed its embassy building in Mexico for more than US$2 million, NK News reports. North Korea has kept a small diplomatic presence in Latin America for decades. The same week its foreign minister rejected a G7 call to give up nuclear weapons.
items.assessment: Selling real estate abroad suggests a cash squeeze or a shrinking diplomatic map. Mexico was one of Pyongyang's few listening posts near the United States.

items.headline: South Korea's foreign minister goes to Beijing before APEC
items.summary: Foreign Minister Cho Hyun travels to Beijing November 13 for two days of talks with China's foreign minister Wang Yi. The agenda covers ties, North Korea and regional issues. A Seoul official said a Trump and Kim meeting at APEC is unlikely, but contact before or after is hard to predict.
items.assessment: Seoul wants Beijing to nudge Pyongyang back to talks before Trump lands in Shenzhen. If China says no, Seoul has few other doors to knock on.

items.headline: Lee will pitch Middle East energy shocks at ASEAN and APEC
items.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will press for regional cooperation on energy supply shocks from the Middle East, his national security adviser said. He holds a Korea and ASEAN summit in Manila on November 16, then the ASEAN Plus Three and East Asia summits on November 17. He meets Thailand's Anutin Charnvirakul and the Philippines' Marcos, but no Japan or China one on one is announced.
items.assessment: The Iran war is now the main agenda item for importers in East Asia, ahead of the South China Sea. The missing Japan and China meetings say more than the ones on the list.

items.headline: Seoul's justice nominee won't say if he would drop charges against Lee
items.summary: Justice minister nominee Lee Yong-cheol would not say if he would drop charges against President Lee Jae Myung. The question turns on whether a special counsel finds prosecutors abused their power. The National Assembly passed that special counsel bill on November 6, and the cabinet takes it up November 17. All five of the president's criminal trials have been paused since he took office in June 2025.
items.assessment: The special counsel could become a legal route to end the president's own trials. The opposition People Power Party will make that its main attack line.

items.headline: Manila tells officials to stop freelancing on China before the summit
items.summary: The Philippine foreign ministry told officials and agencies to avoid unofficial remarks about China and speak with one voice before the ASEAN summit it hosts. On November 12 Global Times, a Chinese state tabloid, said Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro is now isolated and being restrained by his own government. The Philippine military counted 29 Chinese navy and coast guard ships in disputed waters from November 3 to 8.
items.assessment: Manila wants a calm summit to save its code of conduct push. Beijing is using that to paint its harshest critic as sidelined, which may widen splits in the Marcos camp.
items.source: China Global South Project; Global Times; GMA News

alsoNoted.note: New rules let travelers bring home medicine bought abroad.

Seoul's unification minister reads Pyongyang's weapons displays as a message to the South
Global Times: the 'Squad' (US, Japan, Australia, Philippines) pushes Manila onto the front line

items.headline: Russia's deputy prime minister brings 70 businesses to Kabul
items.summary: Alexei Overchuk, a Russian deputy prime minister, met Taliban economic chief Abdul Ghani Baradar in Kabul on November 12. More than 70 Russian business people came along, from transport to drugs to farming. The Taliban invited Russian firms into mining, factories, dry ports and fertilizer plants.
items.assessment: Russia was the first to formally recognize the Taliban in 2025 and now wants a return on it. With Pakistan's border trade frozen, Kabul needs northern partners more than ever.

items.headline: Russia's military alliance turns its focus to Afghanistan
items.summary: At a Moscow summit of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, a Russian led military alliance, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov called for joint action against threats from Afghanistan. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon stressed border security, and leaders signed 18 documents. A five year plan will send equipment from Russia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan to guard Tajikistan's 1,300 km Afghan border.
items.assessment: With Armenia effectively gone, Moscow needs a reason for the alliance to exist. Afghanistan gives it one, while Russia trades with the Taliban at the same time.

items.headline: Kandahar drug company workers protest the Taliban ban on Pakistani medicines
items.summary: Pharmacy and drug company workers protested in Kandahar against a Taliban ban on medicines made in Pakistan. Afghanistan has long relied on Pakistani drugs. The ban comes as Pakistan keeps border trade shut until attacks from Afghan soil stop.
items.assessment: The trade war is now hitting Afghan patients and Pashtun traders in the Taliban's own heartland. That is a rare source of pressure from inside the movement's base.

items.headline: Kazakhstan detains the heads of its wealth fund and railways
items.summary: Kazakh authorities detained the chiefs of Samruk-Kazyna, the national wealth fund that owns most big state companies, and of the national railway company. It is part of a corruption probe announced November 12, The Times of Central Asia reports. Separately, Russian rail limits put up to US$470 million in Kazakh coal exports at risk.
items.assessment: Arresting the man who runs most of the state economy is a political signal from President Tokayev, not just a graft case. It comes as Kazakhstan's export routes through Russia get harder.

items.headline: Researchers say Kazakhstan linked hackers used AI to steal Tajik defense files
items.summary: Security researchers say hackers linked to Kazakhstan used artificial intelligence tools to steal defense documents from Tajikistan. The Times of Central Asia reported the findings on November 11. The two countries are formally allies in the same Russian led military alliance.
items.assessment: Spying among allies in Central Asia is rarely exposed in public. It shows artificial intelligence lowering the cost of state hacking for smaller countries.

items.headline: At least 12 police killed in one day in Pakistan's northwest
items.summary: Dawn, Pakistan's main English paper, says in an editorial that at least 12 police were killed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on November 11. Two officers died in an attack on a patrol in Swabi. On November 13 Peshawar police banned private jirgas, traditional councils, citing gun violence.
items.assessment: Police, not soldiers, are taking the brunt of the militant campaign. That weakens daily state control in the province bordering Afghanistan while Islamabad focuses on air strikes.

items.headline: Bangladesh garment owners threaten closures as the state sells cheap rice to workers
items.summary: Bangladesh's garment factory owners said they will shut units if worker unrest continues, The Daily Star reports. The government will sell rice to garment workers at 30 taka a kilo under its subsidized sales program. The central bank also sold US$200 million to steady the currency.
items.assessment: Earlier wage concessions did not end the unrest. Subsidized rice is a stopgap that shows Dhaka fears a wider labor crisis in its main export industry.

items.headline: Cuba removes provincial chiefs as its government overhaul begins
items.summary: Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia, governor of Camagüey province, resigned on November 10, citing unnamed errors. President Díaz-Canel accepted it, and vice governor Yennis León Mayedo is acting governor. ADN Cuba, a Miami based outlet, reports Las Tunas lost its governor the same day. A local chief in Ciego de Ávila was also removed over problems at a food program and a cooperative.
items.assessment: The removals land the week Law 186, the law that reshapes the government, took effect. Blaming provincial officials for blackouts and a sugar harvest at about 17% of plan shields Havana's ministers from the same scrutiny.

items.headline: Rubio says Cuba has no future, Díaz-Canel says the US won't decide it
items.summary: On November 9 the State Department released a video of Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying Cuba has no future under its current political and economic model. He said the embargo lifts only with political and economic freedom. Trump again called Cuba a failed nation the same day. Díaz-Canel answered on X that the island's future will never be decided from the north.
items.assessment: The public exchange came days after reports that Havana quietly met US officials in New York. Loud rhetoric on both sides may be cover for talks neither government wants to admit to its own base.

items.headline: After Yoani Sánchez's release, pressure shifts to other dissidents
items.summary: ADN Cuba reports that state security is pushing Henry Constantín, a Camagüey journalist, to leave the country, according to his partner. Jailed rapper Maykel Castillo, known as Osorbo, has a fever and a severe leg infection. Political prisoner Carlos Michael Morales asked for a humanitarian visa, citing heart problems.
items.assessment: Pushing critics into exile is cheaper for Havana than jailing them, since exile draws less foreign attention. Watch whether Constantín leaves, because that would empty one more province of independent reporters.

items.headline: Cuba's street dollar slips after crossing 930 pesos
items.summary: The informal dollar rate, tracked daily by the independent site elTOQUE, stood at 930 Cuban pesos on November 9 after weeks of rises. Directorio Cubano reported further broad drops in the dollar and euro on November 11 and 12. No source gives a clear cause.
items.assessment: A few days of decline do not make a trend, as the outlet itself warns. If the drop holds, it may reflect families holding off on dollar purchases while they wait to see what the US and Havana contacts produce.

alsoNoted.note: Timed to the pope's South America tour.

alsoNoted.note: Housing squats are a quiet sign of the shortage.

items.headline: Brazilian court orders Meta to pay $1.3 million over unequal treatment of candidates
items.summary: A Brazilian court ordered Meta, owner of Facebook and Instagram, to pay about US$1.3 million for treating presidential candidates unequally during the election, EFE reported on November 11. The full ruling details were not available to us.
items.assessment: The ruling hands both camps a talking point about the contested runoff. It also signals Brazil's courts will keep policing platforms after the vote, not just during it.

items.headline: Lula flies to Manila for a rare ASEAN opening speech, cabinet still unnamed
items.summary: Lula left the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, on the night of November 12 for the Philippines. He makes a state visit on November 14. He is invited to speak at the opening of the ASEAN summit on November 15, a slot usually kept for the host. Brazil asked in January to become a full ASEAN dialogue partner, alongside the US, Japan, Canada and South Korea.
items.assessment: Trade with Southeast Asia grew from about $3 billion in 2003 to $38 billion in 2025. So Lula is courting a market that is not tied to Washington or Beijing. The cost at home is a longer wait for his Finance minister, which keeps markets nervous.

alsoNoted.headline: Pernambuco press: Lula leaning toward a technical Finance pick, with Haddad possibly moving to the BNDES development bank
alsoNoted.note: Speculation, no confirmation from the presidency. Outside the window, included as background.

items.headline: Bolivia asks Mexico if it gave asylum to ex vice president García Linera
items.summary: Bolivia's foreign ministry asked Mexico on November 12 to say whether it granted political asylum to Álvaro García Linera, Evo Morales's former vice president. He faces murder and torture charges in the Hotel Las Américas case and was summoned to testify on November 11. He told Bolivian TV he has been in Mexico as an asylee since October 31.
items.assessment: Bolivian lawmakers already talk of extradition, which would test Mexico's long habit of sheltering leftist exiles. It also sets up a new quarrel between Sheinbaum and a right turning neighbor.

items.headline: Venezuela reopens applications for Supreme Court judges until November 18
items.summary: The National Assembly's judicial nominations committee extended its deadline by seven days. Applications for the Supreme Court, the courts inspectorate and the judicial school run from November 12 to 18 in Caracas. The opposition backed US plan calls for new courts before elections.
items.assessment: Who sits on the new Supreme Court will decide whether any election held in six months can be challenged. A quiet paperwork extension is where that fight is being decided.

items.headline: Venezuela tightens visits to Machado ally Perkins Rocha as Ramo Verde hunger strike grows
items.summary: Vente Venezuela, María Corina Machado's party, says police were ordered to limit visits to its leader Perkins Rocha, who is under house arrest. At the Ramo Verde military prison, 34 soldiers are on an indefinite hunger strike, and two women joined on November 11. Relatives say prisoners are denied water and health care.
items.assessment: These cases test whether the reconciliation talks the G7 endorsed on November 11 reach people still in custody. Tightening rules on Machado's own lawyer while those talks go on is a signal to her camp.

items.headline: Venezuelan oil retirees block PDVSA headquarters over $720 million pension debt
items.summary: Retirees of PDVSA, the state oil company, blocked its Caracas offices on November 10, demanding a pension fund debt their spokespeople put at $720 million. Teachers, nurses and professors plan a 12 hour national strike on November 16 over year end bonuses. Acting president Delcy Rodríguez has not answered their demands.
items.assessment: A US audit found about $12 billion in Venezuelan export money held under US control this year. That makes unpaid pensions a political problem for Washington's plan too, not just for Caracas.

items.headline: Two Indigenous Piaroa killed as ELN and FARC dissidents clash inside Venezuela
items.summary: Two Piaroa Indigenous people were killed in fighting between the ELN, a Colombian guerrilla group, and FARC dissidents in Venezuela's Bolívar state, NTN24 reported on November 11. Rights groups also report threats and killings of Indigenous people in Apure and Amazonas. A November 10 report described how Colombia took part in Venezuela's bombing of an ELN camp.
items.assessment: Pushing the ELN out of Apure seems to be pushing the fight south into Indigenous mining land. Colombian help with Venezuelan strikes would be a sharp turn after decades of mutual suspicion.

items.headline: Bukele sets up an operating base in Haiti's national stadium
items.summary: El Salvador's president Nayib Bukele announced on November 13 a base at Haiti's main stadium in Port-au-Prince, EFE reported. On November 11 Haiti's government said it was regaining territory with Salvadoran help. Earlier, gang leader Mathias Saintil died in Cité Soleil after an explosive drone strike, according to a rights group, though police said he was shot.
items.assessment: A permanent base suggests Salvadoran troops plan to stay, still outside the UN backed Gang Suppression Force. Conflicting accounts of who killed whom show how little anyone outside can check these operations.

items.headline: Paraguay's new president freezes nonessential state purchases
items.summary: President Pedro Alliana suspended nonessential public purchases on November 10 and demanded a report within 72 hours. On November 11 business groups pressed him for strict austerity in the 2027 budget and an end to perks. Alliana took over after the Senate removed Santiago Peña over the Ueno Bank collapse.
items.assessment: Austerity lets Alliana distance himself from Peña while paying back depositors and pensioners. Cuts to public services could turn the bank crisis into street anger at his own government.

items.headline: US moves to take $1.2 billion of North Korea's Binance loot
items.summary: The Justice Department announced steps on November 12 to disrupt North Korean crypto theft. Stablecoin firms Tether and Circle locked $2.7 billion after the October 29 Binance hack. Bloomberg reports that a court let the Justice Department seize or freeze $1.2 billion of it. The FBI blamed that $6.3 billion theft on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacking group.
items.assessment: Most of the money is still out of reach, and Binance has already covered customer losses itself. So the real test is whether frozen stablecoins become a standard tool, which gives two private firms a police like role.
items.source: US Department of Justice; Bloomberg (via Techmeme); The Record

items.headline: Gootloader malware disrupted in an international operation
items.summary: The Justice Department says an international operation disrupted Gootloader. Gootloader is malware that hides in poisoned search results and opens the door for ransomware gangs. The release itself was not opened, so partners and arrests are unknown.
items.assessment: Gootloader is a first stage tool that other criminals rent. Taking it down should cut some ransomware entry points for a while, but past takedowns of similar tools lasted only months.

items.headline: Krebs profiles Qilin, now the most active ransomware gang
items.summary: Security journalist Brian Krebs published an investigation into who runs Qilin. Qilin is a ransomware group that rents its tools to affiliates and is now the busiest such gang in the world. The piece names a likely operator.
items.assessment: Public naming often comes before charges or sanctions from the Treasury. It can also push the gang to rebrand under a new name.

White House picks Palantir's security chief to run CISA
alsoNoted.note: Michael LoSapio. CISA is the federal civilian cyber defense agency. He now needs a Senate that Democrats take over in January.

items.headline: Dark web drug sweep nets more than 350 arrests worldwide
items.summary: The Justice Department and Europol, the EU police agency, announced Operation TorNado against opioid and fentanyl sellers on the dark web. The FBI led JCODE task force ran the US side. Officials report more than 350 arrests and over $234 million seized, along with drugs and weapons.
items.assessment: The size of the cash haul shows dark web drug markets now run like payment businesses. Seizing money and crypto is becoming as central as seizing drugs.

alsoNoted.headline: Attorney General Blanche says DOJ has not decided if Alice Huang was a spy
alsoNoted.note: New since the Epoch Times item: Blanche is now on record and says the FBI is investigating.

items.headline: CFTC chair reversed policy to allow perpetual bets on Kalshi
items.summary: The New York Times reports how Michael Selig, chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, reversed agency policy. The change lets Kalshi and similar platforms offer perpetual crypto and stock contracts, which never expire. Securities and Exchange Commission staff had raised concerns.
items.assessment: This opens a path for stock like trading outside SEC rules. A Democratic Congress is likely to make it an oversight target early next year.

alsoNoted.note: Indicted by a South Florida grand jury.

items.headline: Democrats and industry groups push immigration changes after the midterms
items.summary: States Newsroom reports that Democrats and business groups are pressing for immigration changes now that the midterms are over. The article was not opened, so the specific asks are not confirmed here.
items.assessment: Business groups joining Democrats points to work visas and farm labor as the likely first deal. Miller's own list includes tighter visas for students and temporary workers, so this sets up an early clash.

alsoNoted.headline: IBM ends most H-1B and green card sponsorship in its consulting arm
alsoNoted.note: H-1B is the main US work visa for skilled foreign workers. A large employer quitting it is an early sign of the $100,000 fee biting, though that fee is still tied up in court.

items.headline: Congo's president signs the referendum law critics tie to a third term
items.summary: President Félix Tshisekedi signed a law on November 11 that lets the president call a referendum and a constituent assembly to change the constitution. Parliament passed it in June and the Constitutional Court cleared it in July. The constitution limits presidents to two five year terms, and Tshisekedi's second term ends in 2028. He denies seeking a third term but said in May he would accept one if the people asked.
items.assessment: The law can be triggered by a 'major dysfunction' of the state. A country with rebels holding much of the east and the worst Ebola outbreak of its kind could be argued to qualify. That hands the Rwanda backed M23 rebels, who already say Tshisekedi wants to stay in power, a fresh argument at the negotiating table.
items.source: BusinessDay (South Africa), background from Africanews, July 29

items.headline: Islamic State reportedly rewards its West African branch for raiding army stockpiles
items.summary: Premium Times is a leading Nigerian investigative paper. It reported on November 12 that the Islamic State is giving incentives to ISWAP to target military stockpiles in Nigeria and nearby countries. ISWAP is the Islamic State's West Africa Province, based around Lake Chad. We could only see the headline, so the source of the finding and the type of reward are not confirmed.
items.assessment: If accurate, army depots become the group's main supply line, so each overrun base arms the next attack. That risk grows as Nigeria heads into a national election early next year, when troops get pulled toward security for polling.

items.headline: Attacks on Nigerian campaign events grow as a challenger targets Tinubu's oil loans
items.summary: Nigeria's House of Representatives said on November 12 it will investigate attacks on political rallies and supporters. Suspected thugs damaged vehicles at a town hall venue of the NDC party in Lagos, and the ruling APC party condemned the attacks on November 13. Separately, a campaign group for Oyo State governor Seyi Makinde demanded a probe of 11.2 trillion naira in loans backed by future crude oil sales. Makinde is challenging President Bola Tinubu.
items.assessment: Loans repaid in oil lock up future export income, so the issue speaks to voters who feel no benefit from oil. With Atiku Abubakar's nomination tied up in court, Makinde has room to become the main challenger, and campaign violence tends to rise as the field narrows.

items.headline: IMF sets conditions before Senegal's $2.2 billion loan
items.summary: The International Monetary Fund said on November 12 that Senegal must first set a budget framework and finish corrective steps. Only then will its board approve a $2.2 billion program. Senegal's IMF lending was frozen after a 2024 audit found the previous government had hidden part of the country's debt and deficit.
items.assessment: Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko's government built its brand on sovereignty, so visible IMF conditions are politically costly at home. The deal also decides whether Senegal can keep borrowing on markets without a messy debt restructuring.

items.headline: Ghana's 2027 budget unveils a $10 billion 'New Economy' plan
items.summary: Ghana announced a four year, $10 billion investment plan in its 2027 budget on November 13. It targets farming, energy, technology and manufacturing. Ghana defaulted on most of its debt in 2022 and has been under a $3 billion IMF bailout since 2023.
items.assessment: The key unknown is how the plan is paid for. If it leans on new borrowing just as IMF oversight winds down, it would repeat the spending pattern that led to the 2022 default.

items.headline: Ivory Coast warns El Niño could cut its cocoa crop by a quarter
items.summary: Ivory Coast's weather agency said on November 11 that drought and heat from El Niño could cut cocoa output by up to 25%. Ivory Coast is the world's largest cocoa grower. The damage would come from lost pods and stressed trees.
items.assessment: Ivory Coast and Ghana set fixed prices for farmers, so a world price spike mostly helps the state marketing boards while farmers simply sell less. Tree damage also means the loss can carry into the following season.

items.headline: South Africa's hung councils face a left coalition offer and Treasury penalties
items.summary: A group called the Council of the Left offered the ANC coalition talks on November 13, on condition that it drop what it called reactionary partners. The same day Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana said the Treasury will keep withholding money from badly run municipalities. Both come as many councils have no majority after the ANC's worst local election.
items.assessment: Shaky coalitions are often the councils that manage money worst, so Treasury penalties could land hardest where governing is already weakest. That cuts water and power services and feeds anger ahead of the 2029 national vote.

alsoNoted.headline: Press groups demand release of a detained Nigerian investigative journalist
alsoNoted.note: Reporter Ojukwu of the Foundation for Investigative Journalism is held on defamation charges. The Committee to Protect Journalists and a Nigerian press center called for release.

alsoNoted.note: Activist Vigario Luis Balanta. The probe opened after pressure from civic groups and the media.

alsoNoted.note: A nonprofit alleges corruption and sanctions evasion in logging and urges tougher trade rules.

items.headline: Congo's Ebola count passes 11,100, but weekly growth slows
items.summary: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control is the EU's disease agency. It reported on November 12 that Congo has 11,114 confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola cases and 5,433 deaths in eight provinces. That is about 370 new cases and 200 deaths in a week, down from about 470 cases and 240 deaths the week before. Kenya has nine cases and two deaths, Nigeria one imported case, and Uganda's outbreak is over.
items.assessment: A slowdown in reported cases looks the same as a slowdown in testing. With armed attacks scattering patients in North Kivu, part of the drop may be cases that nobody is counting.
items.source: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control

items.headline: Ebola patients fled clinics after an Islamic State linked raid in North Kivu
items.summary: Africa CDC, the African Union's public health agency, said a November 5 attack on Cantine Aloya in North Kivu was reportedly carried out by the ADF. The ADF is a Ugandan born armed group that has pledged loyalty to the Islamic State. Health facilities were hit and hundreds of patients with confirmed or suspected Ebola fled. On November 12 the agency warned that attacks on health workers could undo six months of progress.
items.assessment: Each patient who flees untreated can start new chains of infection outside contact tracing. The effect would show up in case counts two to three weeks later, around early December.
items.source: Africa CDC statement via allAfrica, plus BusinessDay (South Africa)

items.headline: Kenya discharges its last Ebola patient and starts a 42 day clock
items.summary: Kenya released its last Ebola patient on November 11 after nine cases since early October. It now begins a 42 day watch, two full incubation periods, before it can be declared free of the disease. No new Kenyan case has been reported since October 19.
items.assessment: If nothing new appears, Kenya could be declared free around late December. That would keep East Africa's main air hub off the US travel ban that already applies to recent visitors to Congo.

items.headline: Fewer pregnant women in Nigeria are getting HIV treatment
items.summary: Premium Times reported on November 12 that HIV treatment among pregnant women in Nigeria has declined. Treatment during pregnancy is what keeps mothers from passing the virus to their babies. We could only see the headline, so the figures and stated cause are not confirmed.
items.assessment: Nigeria has long had one of the world's highest counts of babies born with HIV. Whether US aid cuts since 2025 are behind the drop is unknown from what we saw. But this is the kind of measurable cost that would show up first.

alsoNoted.headline: UK health agency: US has 72 confirmed human H5 bird flu cases since 2024, 42 tied to dairy cattle
alsoNoted.note: Context only, figures as of October 15. The weekly report lists no mpox, Marburg, cholera or polio alerts.

alsoNoted.headline: Africa CDC: the continent is 'not winning' against Ebola
alsoNoted.note: Background. Over 40 health ministers agreed to keep borders open. Nigeria's case was genetically close to Kenya's strain, though Nigeria's health minister said that does not prove a direct link.

items.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns, finance chief steps in
items.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, chief executive and board member on November 12, effective immediately, according to the company's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing gives no reason. Chief financial officer Colette Kress becomes interim chief executive, and director Harvey Jones becomes the board's first chair. Huang had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a woman some US officials suspect of spying for China, and the board had opened an investigation. Attorney General Blanche said the same day that the Justice Department has not concluded she was a spy. Nvidia still plans to report earnings on November 17.
items.assessment: The world's most valuable chip company lost its founder in one day, with no reason given and the spy question still open. Expect sharp market moves around the November 17 earnings report and louder calls in Congress for tighter chip controls on China.
items.source: Nvidia filing with the SEC; Reuters

items.headline: OpenAI backs a bipartisan push to limit China's AI chip access
items.summary: Bloomberg reports OpenAI told lawmakers it will support a bipartisan effort in Congress to restrict China's access to AI chips and chipmaking tools. The Financial Times says China hawks and Big Tech critics are building a joint coalition on export controls.
items.assessment: Chip limits are one of the few areas where a Democratic Congress and the White House could agree. OpenAI gains by limiting Chinese rivals, and Nvidia, which sells to China, is the obvious loser.

items.headline: DOJ probes could sweep up Nvidia
items.summary: Semafor reports US officials say several Justice Department investigations could reach Nvidia, the top AI chip maker. One is an antitrust probe. Two others focus on Megaspeed and Supermicro, firms tied to how chips moved abroad.
items.assessment: Probes give Washington leverage over Nvidia while chip export bills move. The company's China sales strategy now runs through prosecutors as well as Congress.

items.headline: Chinese AI firms rush to rent Nvidia chips in overseas data centers
items.summary: Reuters reports that Chinese AI companies are hurrying to lock in Nvidia cloud capacity abroad. Sources say they fear stricter US enforcement after the Alice Huang spy scandal.
items.assessment: Renting chips abroad is the main gap in current export rules. That makes cloud rentals the likely next target for any bill Congress writes.

items.headline: Young victims of Grok's sexualized images seek to hold xAI liable
items.summary: Bloomberg reports that young people whose childhood photos were sexualized by Grok, the chatbot from Elon Musk's xAI, are seeking legal accountability from the company.
items.assessment: Cases like this test whether AI makers are shielded like platforms or liable like publishers. Democrats have already said AI liability is on their agenda.

alsoNoted.note: The FCC is the Federal Communications Commission. The parts are transceivers used in data centers.

items.summary: States Newsroom reports the Trump administration is going back to court to try again on ending automatic citizenship for children born in the US. The article was not opened, so the court and case are not confirmed here.
items.assessment: A second round signals the White House expects to lose fights in Congress and is betting on courts it sees as friendlier. Any new ruling would land just as Democrats take over the committees that oversee immigration.

items.headline: Lawyers accuse a Kansas judge of religious bias to revive an abortion case
items.summary: Lawyers defending a Kansas anti abortion law are trying to reopen the case by accusing the judge of religious discrimination. The report comes from Kansas Reflector via States Newsroom. The body was not opened.
items.assessment: Attacking a judge's faith is a new way to reopen a lost case. If it works in Kansas, expect copies in other states where courts struck down abortion limits.

alsoNoted.note: Seen in the opened DOJ press list. A new indictment ties them to Kata'ib Hizballah, an Iraqi militia, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard. It includes a September 2026 plot at a British air force base. Dated November 10 and not in earlier editions.

items.headline: Japan may lack time to scatter US forces before war
items.summary: Christopher Denzel, writing in War on the Rocks (a US national security site), says Japan's biggest problem in a Taiwan crisis is the clock. US forces must leave crowded bases before the first missile salvo. But emergency use of private land may only open after an attack starts. Normal peacetime access takes three to more than five months.
items.assessment: The weak point is paperwork in Tokyo, not missiles. That makes landowners and the 110,000 people on Japan's Sakishima islands, about 70 miles from Taiwan, a pressure point that a rival could target to slow approvals.

items.headline: Retired US nuclear officer: give China status, not demands
items.summary: Nicole Klingensmith is a retired Air Force officer with about 20 years in nuclear jobs. She argues that China resists arms control mainly because it wants to be treated as an equal. She says asking Beijing to accept limits first will keep failing. She suggests Washington offer recognition as a cheap bargaining chip before the planned Trump and Xi meeting.
items.assessment: This flips the usual view of China's nuclear buildup as pure threat. A weakened Trump facing a Democratic Congress could trade symbolic respect for nuclear talks at low cost, though critics will call it a giveaway.

items.headline: Pentagon urged to brew fuel and food at the front
items.summary: Two authors in War on the Rocks say the military should build small mobile plants that use engineered microbes to make fuel, plastics and food near the fighting. They point to supply strains in the Iran war and the USS Abraham Lincoln's record deployment. The Pentagon has put nearly $1 billion into this field since 2020, mostly into central sites.
items.assessment: The pitch sells biotech as a way to shorten fragile supply lines, not as a cheaper product. One author cofounded a biomanufacturing company, so the call for the government to be the main buyer also serves his industry.

items.headline: Munitions money is flowing, but small suppliers have vanished
items.summary: A War on the Rocks analysis says the Pentagon is sending a record demand signal for missiles and shells. Turning that into deliveries depends on suppliers several layers below the big contractors. Many of those small firms disappeared over the last two decades. The piece also asks whether China's grip on critical minerals could halt production.
items.assessment: Bigger budgets alone will not refill stocks drained by the Iran war. A Democratic Congress that now controls spending may find the bottleneck is a missing parts maker, not money.

items.headline: Gold breaks below $3,900 as traders eye a bigger Fed hike
items.summary: Gold fell more than 2.5% on Thursday to about $3,870 an ounce, a level not seen in months. Traders priced about a 90% chance the Fed, the US central bank, raises rates in December, and about 10% for a half point jump. Gold climbed back above $3,900 on Friday but is still set for a sharp weekly loss.
items.assessment: Gold usually rises in wartime. Its slide shows markets now fear US interest rates more than the Iran war, so the war reaches most households through borrowing costs.

items.headline: Bitcoin hits its lowest level since August, down 16% this year
items.summary: Bitcoin fell below $73,500 on November 11, its lowest since mid August. The trigger was hotter October inflation and Fed governor Christopher Waller saying a half point December hike should be considered. Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan also hinted at faster hikes.
items.assessment: Bitcoin is trading like a tech stock that hates high rates, not like a wartime safe haven. Gold and bitcoin falling together means money is leaving anything that pays no interest.

items.headline: Moody's puts the Iran war's cost near $2,000 per household
items.summary: Veronique de Rugy, an economist writing for the libertarian magazine Reason, says Republicans lost because they pushed prices up through tariffs, the war and immigration raids. She cites gasoline rising from $2.98 to $4.15 between February and Election Day, with diesel at $6.28. She cites Moody's, the ratings firm, putting the war's cost at about $2,000 per household.
items.assessment: She rejects Vice President Vance's claim that the war alone explains the losses, because it lets tariffs off the hook. That sets up a fight on the right over whether to end the trade war or the shooting war first.
